data.hypothesis: The best visible T1 result used a 4096-element input tile and measured 7.81568 µs over three samples, while two 128-element-tile variants measured about 44.2 µs. This candidate tests a larger 8192-element tile while retaining the 128-thread shared-memory reduction tree and int64 partials: for n=4,194,304 it emits 512 rather than 1024 input partials and should still use two kernels. Reduced CTA count and finalizer work may help, but greater serial accumulation per thread or lower parallelism may offset that; larger n retains bounded recursive stages. These are whole-call performance hypotheses, not measured conclusions.

memory_lessons.applicability: Use this as a tile-size comparison only; whole-call measurements do not isolate the source of the difference.
memory_lessons.claim: The 4096-element-tile candidate was valid and measured 7.81568 µs over three samples. The 128-element-tile candidates were also valid and measured about 44.2 µs; the available results do not establish which code change caused the difference.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure this 8192-element tile with repeated full-call timings and compare it with the 4096-element candidate under the same protocol.

data.notes: No build, correctness check, or measurement was run in this proposal. The candidate checks the pointers it uses, handles n == 0 without reading scratch, writes each partial before consuming it, and accumulates in long long before narrowing the true total. No failed-variant diagnostics are available; controller validation and repeated full-call measurement are needed.
transformations: Changed the bounded input tile to 8192 elements per 128-thread CTA, retaining the shared-memory modulo reduction tree and accumulating each thread's strided values in long long.
Uses two packed long-long scratch buffers for initial partials and recursive stages; reduces recursively while the partial count exceeds 1024, then writes the final result directly to out.
Uses a one-CTA direct reduction only for n <= 128, handles n == 0 by writing zero, checks required pointers, and does not depend on scratch initialization.
